question: If I work while I'm incarcerated, in a prison job or on work release, how is my pay set, what can the state deduct from my earnings and in what order, and what do I get back when I'm released?

groups: employed and paid by the District
Director of the Department of Corrections

gold_sections.why: Work release earnings: the Mayor may have wages collected, less payroll deductions required or authorized by law, into a trust fund, protected from garnishment, and paid out for six listed (unranked) purposes, including room and board capped at the lesser of 20% or $4 a day; the balance is paid at the end of confinement.

How work release pay is set: a prisoner working in the free community is not an agent, employee or servant of the D.C. government unless employed and paid by the District, so the wage comes from the outside employer; the code sets no work release wage.

Release payment: suitable clothing and, in the Mayor's discretion, up to $100 on release from a penal or correctional institution under D.C. government jurisdiction (not Bureau of Prisons facilities).
Jail labor: sentenced Jail inmates may be employed under Council regulations (no wage in the statute), with the proceeds applied to the expenses of their trial and conviction.

People sentenced to incarceration under the D.C. Code (felons) are designated to Bureau of Prisons facilities and are subject to federal law and regulation, so their prison pay and deductions are federal.

Who can get work release (misdemeanor terms of 1 year or less, nonpayment of fine or contempt, probation revocation, or special circumstances), that the sentencing judge or, after 1/3 of the sentence, the Board of Parole may grant it, and that it is for working at or seeking employment.

Work release may be recommended or requested at sentencing and requested from the sentencing court or the DOC Director at any time afterward; only the sentencing court, the DOC Director or the Board of Parole (under 24-241.01) may order it.
Support deducted under 24-241.06 is paid through the court clerks; with no support order or judgment, the welfare agency reports the amount needed for the prisoner's dependents.

Victims of violent crime assessments of an offender indigent at sentencing must be paid from wages or compensation received while incarcerated; assessments are collected as fines and DOC monitors collection from incarcerated defendants.

DOC, with Council approval, may establish and conduct industries, farms and other activities for inmates; DOC must return personal identification documents on release from the Central Detention Facility.

For residents released from the Jail between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m., DOC must first ensure housing or shelter, return of the clothing worn at intake (or suitable street clothing), at least a 7-day supply of prescription medications, and transportation.
The Council may issue rules and regulations for the Department of Corrections' administration of the work release program, where the program's details are left.

nuggets.text: Work release is available mainly to people serving misdemeanor (or municipal-regulation) sentences of 1 year or less, people jailed for not paying a fine or for contempt, and people jailed after probation revocation; the sentencing judge, or the Board of Parole after a third of the sentence has been served, may grant it so the person can work at a job or look for one.
nuggets.quote: whenever the judge of the sentencing court is satisfied that the ends of justice and the best interests of society as well as of such person would be subserved thereby or whenever after service by the person of 1/3 of his or her sentence, the Board of Parole is satisfied that the ends of justice and the best interests of society as well as of the sentenced person would be served thereby, be granted the privilege of a work release for the purpose of working at his employment or seeking employment

nuggets.text: People sentenced to incarceration under the D.C. Code for felonies are placed in Bureau of Prisons facilities and are subject to the federal laws and regulations that apply to federal prisoners, so their prison pay, deductions and release money follow federal rules.
nuggets.quote: shall be designated by the Bureau of Prisons to a penal or correctional facility operated or contracted for by the Bureau of Prisons, for such term of imprisonment as the court may direct. Such persons shall be subject to any law or regulation applicable to persons committed for violations of laws of the United States consistent with the sentence imposed.

nuggets.text: No statute sets a wage for D.C. Jail work: people sentenced to the Jail may be employed at labor under regulations prescribed by the D.C. Council, and the proceeds may be applied to the expenses of their trial and conviction.
nuggets.quote: may be employed at such labor and under such regulations as may be prescribed by the Council of the District of Columbia and the proceeds thereof applied to defray the expenses of the trial and conviction of any such person

nuggets.text: A prisoner working in the free community on work release is not an agent, employee or servant of the D.C. government unless the District itself employs and pays them, so work release pay is the wage paid by the outside employer; the code sets no separate work release wage.
nuggets.quote: Except when employed and paid by the District of Columbia for the performance of work for the District of Columbia government, no prisoner employed in the free community under the provisions of this subchapter shall, while working in such employment in the free community or going to or from such employment, be deemed to be an agent, employee, or servant of the District of Columbia government.

nuggets.text: The Mayor may include in an individual work release plan the collection of the prisoner's wages and other income, or require them to be surrendered, minus payroll deductions required or authorized by law, and deposit the rest in a trust fund account; payroll deductions therefore come off before the money reaches the trust fund.
nuggets.quote: provisions for the collection of the wages, salary, earnings, and other income of each gainfully employed prisoner when paid, or require that the same be surrendered when received, less payroll deductions required or authorized by law, and to deposit the amount so received in a trust fund account in the Treasury of the United States

nuggets.text: While the prisoner is serving the term, work release wages held by the employer or the Mayor cannot be garnished or attached.
nuggets.quote: Such wages, salary, or earnings in the hands of either the employer or the Mayor during such prisoner's terms shall not be subject to garnishment or attachment.

nuggets.text: The work release plan may provide for paying money out of the trust fund for any or all of six listed purposes; the statute lists them but does not rank them in an order of priority.
nuggets.quote: The Mayor is further authorized in individual work release plans to provide for disbursements from the trust fund account established under this section for any or all of the following purposes

nuggets.text: First and second listed: room and board, which may not exceed the lesser of 20% of the prisoner's earnings or $4 per day; and necessary travel to and from work or other business plus the prisoner's incidental expenses.
nuggets.quote: (1) the payment of an amount not to exceed the lesser of 20% of the prisoner's earnings, or $4 per day, as the cost of his room and board; (2) necessary travel expenses to and from work or other business and incidental expenses of the prisoner

nuggets.text: Third and fourth listed: support of the prisoner's dependents, and support of minor children under a court order.
nuggets.quote: (3) support of the prisoner's dependents, if any; (4) support of minor children pursuant to court order

nuggets.text: Fifth and sixth listed: court fines or forfeitures, and the prisoner's debts (in full or ratably) that the prisoner acknowledged in writing or that have been reduced to judgment.
nuggets.quote: (5) payment of court fines or forfeitures; or (6) payment, either in full or ratably, of the prisoner's debts which have been acknowledged by him in writing or have been reduced to judgment

nuggets.text: Whatever remains after those payments is paid to the prisoner when the period of confinement is completed.
nuggets.quote: The balance of such earnings, if any there be after payments therefrom for the foregoing purposes, shall be paid to the prisoner upon the completion of the period during which he is subject to confinement.

nuggets.text: Support payments from work release earnings go through the court clerks; where there is no support order or judgment, the social services (public welfare) agency investigates and reports to the Mayor how much the prisoner's dependents need.
nuggets.quote: Payments for support pursuant to § 24-241.06 shall be made through the clerks of the respective courts. In cases where there is no outstanding court order of support or judgment against the prisoner, the Director, Department of Public Welfare, or his designated agent, shall, after investigation, report to the Mayor the amounts deemed necessary for support of the prisoner's dependents.

nuggets.text: If an offender was indigent at sentencing and later receives wages or compensation while incarcerated in a Department of Corrections facility or elsewhere, the crime victims compensation assessments must be paid from those wages.
nuggets.quote: is incarcerated in a facility of the Department of Corrections or elsewhere and receives wages or compensation therein, the amount of assessments under this section shall be paid from such salary, wages, or other compensation

nuggets.text: On release from a penal or correctional institution under the jurisdiction of the D.C. government (not a Bureau of Prisons facility), the Mayor may provide suitable clothing and, at the Mayor's discretion, a sum of money of no more than $100.
nuggets.quote: upon his release from a penal or correctional institution under the jurisdiction of the government of the District of Columbia with suitable clothing and, in the discretion of the Mayor, a sum of money, which shall not exceed $100

nuggets.text: On release from the Central Detention Facility (the D.C. Jail), the Department of Corrections must return any personal identification documents it collected, such as driver's licenses, birth certificates and Social Security cards.
nuggets.quote: Return to an inmate, upon the inmate's release from the Central Detention Facility, any personal identification documents collected from the inmate, including driver's licenses, birth certificates, and Social Security cards

office.value: The Mayor collects work release wages into the trust fund and sets disbursements in each individual work release plan
The outside employer pays work release wages; the prisoner is a District employee only when the District employs and pays them
The sentencing judge, or the Board of Parole after a third of the sentence is served, grants work release
The D.C. Council prescribes the regulations for Jail labor

ordered_list.item: Payroll deductions required or authorized by law come off first, before the earnings are deposited in the trust fund (fixed by the statute)
Listed purpose (1): room and board, capped at the lesser of 20% of earnings or $4 per day (statutory listing order only; the six purposes are not ranked)
Listed purpose (2): necessary travel to and from work or other business, and incidental expenses (listing order only, not a priority)
Listed purpose (3): support of the prisoner's dependents (listing order only, not a priority)
Listed purpose (4): support of minor children under a court order (listing order only, not a priority)
Listed purpose (5): court fines or forfeitures (listing order only, not a priority)
Listed purpose (6): debts acknowledged in writing or reduced to judgment, in full or ratably (listing order only, not a priority)
Balance paid to the prisoner at the end of confinement, after the plan's payments (fixed by the statute)

fee.value: room and board: no more than the lesser of 20% of earnings or $4 per day

amount.value: release money: up to $100, at the Mayor's discretion, plus suitable clothing, on release from a D.C.-run institution

answer: D.C. felons serve time in Bureau of Prisons facilities, so federal law, not the D.C. Code, sets their pay, deductions and release money [N2]. No statute sets a wage for D.C. Jail jobs: sentenced inmates may work under Council regulations, with the proceeds applied to their trial and conviction costs [N3]. Work release, mainly for misdemeanor sentences of a year or less, may be granted by the sentencing judge or, after a third of the sentence, the Board of Parole [N1]. On work release your employer pays you; you are not a District employee unless the District employs and pays you [N16]. After payroll deductions required or authorized by law, your plan may collect your pay into a trust fund [N4] that cannot be garnished [N5]. It may then pay for any or all of these unranked purposes [N6]: room and board (the lesser of 20% of earnings or $4 a day) and travel and incidental expenses [N7]; your dependents' support and court-ordered child support [N9], paid through the court clerks; without a support order, the welfare agency reports what they need [N12]; and court fines or forfeitures and acknowledged or judgment debts, in full or ratably [N10]. Victim assessments you could not pay at sentencing must come from prison wages [N13]. The balance is paid to you when confinement ends [N11]. On release from a D.C.-run facility, you may get suitable clothing and, at the Mayor's discretion, up to $100 [N14]; the Jail must return your ID documents [N15].

out_of_corpus.what: For people serving D.C. felony sentences in Bureau of Prisons custody: prison work assignments and performance pay, Federal Prison Industries pay, the Inmate Financial Responsibility Program that takes payments toward special assessments, restitution, fines and other debts from inmate accounts, and the federal release gratuity, clothing and transportation
out_of_corpus.where: 28 C.F.R. part 545 (inmate work and performance pay; Inmate Financial Responsibility Program), 18 U.S.C. 4121-4129 (Federal Prison Industries), 18 U.S.C. 3624(d) (release gratuity), and Bureau of Prisons program statements

out_of_corpus.what: Subsistence charges and other rules for D.C. felons placed by the Bureau of Prisons in residential reentry centers (halfway houses) while working
out_of_corpus.where: Bureau of Prisons community corrections / residential reentry center policy and contracts

out_of_corpus.what: Pay rates for D.C. Jail work details and industries, the terms of individual work release plans, how the trust fund and inmate accounts are run, and what may be drawn while inside (the statutes leave these to regulations and the Department of Corrections)
out_of_corpus.where: D.C. Municipal Regulations, Title 28 (Corrections, Courts and Criminal Justice), and D.C. Department of Corrections policies on inmate work programs, work release and inmate finance, adopted under D.C. Code 24-201.12, 24-211.02 and 24-241.04

out_of_corpus.what: Standard payroll withholding (income tax, Social Security and Medicare) taken from work release paychecks before they reach the trust fund
out_of_corpus.where: Internal Revenue Code and D.C. income-tax withholding rules (the 'payroll deductions required or authorized by law' in D.C. Code 24-241.06)

out_of_corpus.what: If inmate labor is for a private-sector industry certified to sell goods in interstate commerce: prevailing-wage pay and a cap on total deductions for room and board, family support, victim compensation and taxes
out_of_corpus.where: Prison Industry Enhancement Certification Program, 18 U.S.C. 1761(c), and the Bureau of Justice Assistance PIECP guideline

version_flags: 24-211.02 carries a note that it includes amendments by temporary legislation that expired on September 11, 2026; the corpus shows the temporary-law text. The parts relied on here (subsection (a), industries and farms, and (b)(5), return of identification documents) are not the temporarily amended provisions as far as the corpus shows, but the permanent version in force on 2026-10-10 should be checked.
notes: D.C. has no counties or sheriffs; the Department of Corrections (DOC) runs the D.C. Jail (Central Detention Facility) and the Correctional Treatment Facility, which hold pretrial detainees and sentenced misdemeanants. Since the Revitalization Act (24-101), D.C. Code felons serve their time in Bureau of Prisons facilities under federal law, so for most long-term prisoners the D.C. Code does not govern pay or deductions. The work release subchapter (24-241.01 to 24-241.10) is old and permissive: the Mayor 'is authorized' to collect wages and to provide for disbursements 'for any or all' of six purposes in each individual plan. The statute fixes only the ends of the sequence: payroll deductions 'required or authorized by law' come off before deposit in the trust fund, and the balance goes to the prisoner at the end of confinement; the six purposes in between are numbered but no order of priority is stated, so ordered_list items 2-7 follow statutory listing order only and an answer that says they are unranked is correct. Nugget ids skip N8 because the former N8 (purpose (2), travel and incidental expenses) was merged into N7. Restitution is not listed separately; it could fall under debts 'reduced to judgment' or court-ordered payments. Old agency names: 'Department of Public Welfare' is now the Department of Human Services, 'Corporation Counsel' is now the Attorney General, and the trust fund is described as 'in the Treasury of the United States'. 24-241.09(a): in the subchapter 'Mayor' includes the Mayor's designated agents; 24-241.03: the DOC Director states in writing the terms and conditions of release for work. 24-241.02: the person may request work release from the sentencing court at sentencing, or from the sentencing court or the DOC Director at any time afterward. 24-241.10: a work releasee in the free community is not a District employee unless employed and paid by the District, so pay comes from the outside employer; the code sets no work release wage. The D.C. Minimum Wage Act's definition of 'employee' (32-1002(2)) excludes only certain volunteers, religious lay officers and casual babysitters, with no exclusion for incarcerated workers, so it plausibly reaches a work releasee employed by a private employer; no statute addresses whether it reaches in-custody Jail labor, and the rate itself is CPI-adjusted each July 1 under 32-1003(a)(6), not fixed in the code. 24-201.12 (proceeds of Jail labor applied to trial and conviction expenses) is a 19th-century provision still in the code. 4-516(b)-(c): DOC monitors collection of victim assessments from incarcerated defendants, the Board of Parole considers whether they are paid, and assessments 'shall be collected as fines', so in a work release plan they may fall under purpose (5) (court fines); the statute does not say so expressly. 4-205.20: for public assistance, the Mayor checks whether an imprisoned parent is on work release and how much support is paid. 51-109(6): a work release prisoner employed in the free community cannot claim unemployment benefits for weeks spent as a prisoner. 50-1401.03(a)(1B): D.C. driver's license and ID card application fees are waived for one year after release from Bureau of Prisons custody (and for people in BOP custody at a D.C. halfway house). Time-credit (not pay) benefits for work: misdemeanants may earn up to 3 good time credits a month for work details (24-221.01c); DOC may give meritorious good time for exceptional service in institutional operations (24-221.01a). 24-211.02a(c) (gold, supporting) applies only to residents released between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m.; DOC must otherwise release residents by 10 p.m. Commissary profits go to the Resident Welfare Fund (24-282), not to wages.
